summary: Describes a network management architecture that runs the ISO management services and protocol (CMIS and CMIP) over the Internet protocols. It was meant as an alternative to SNMP, but the approach did not catch on and the RFC is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: ISO wrote a complete network management protocol, but it assumed ISO's own transport protocols. This RFC says how to run the same management protocol over the Internet instead, and records the choices implementers must all make the same way so their equipment can talk to each other.

subtitle: How ISO's network management standards were fitted onto the Internet, over TCP/IP and over OSI.

tldr.problem: ISO's Common Management Information Services and Protocol had become an International Standard, but the standards did not say how to run them over IP networks, and implementers had to agree on the choices.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1189 defines a profile: which protocols each suite uses, which association types may be negotiated, which application context names identify them, and the agreements on CMIS and CMIP services.
tldr.outcome: CMOT is ISO CMIP over TCP/IP and CMIP is ISO CMIP over OSI networks. RFC 1189 revised RFC 1095 and has not been obsoleted, but is Historic.

today: RFC 1189 is a Historic document from October 1990 and has not been obsoleted. It revised RFC 1095 and was written against the final ISO CMIS/CMIP International Standards rather than the draft versions.

sections.title: What CMOT and CMIP Are
sections.content:
RFC 1189 is a revision of RFC 1095, The Common Management Information Services and Protocol over TCP/IP. It defines a network management architecture that uses the International Organization for Standardization's Common Management Information Services and Common Management Information Protocol (CMIS/CMIP) in the Internet. The architecture gives a means by which control and monitoring information can be exchanged between a manager and a remote network element. In particular, the memo defines the means for implementing the International Standard version of CMIS/CMIP on top of both IP-based and OSI-based Internet transport protocols, for the purpose of carrying management information defined in the Internet-standard management information base.

Together with the relevant ISO standards and the companion RFCs that describe the initial structure of management information and the management information base, these documents provide the basis for a comprehensive architecture and system for managing both IP-based and OSI-based internets, and in particular the Internet.

The revision made five changes. The tutorial section on OSI management included in RFC 1095 was removed, on the understanding that it might be published as another RFC after revision. The sections discussing how to interpret requests in the context of Internet MIBs were removed and are now discussed in the OIM-MIB-II draft. The document is based on the final International Standards for CMIS/CMIP, ISO 9595 and 9596, rather than the draft versions. Many of the original agreements in RFC 1095 were accepted and included in the OIW NMSIG implementers agreements, so rather than duplicating them they were removed and the document should be read with ISO 9595/9596 and the OIW Stable Agreements document. And the Association Negotiation described in RFC 1095 was changed to align with current international and national agreements, while retaining backwards compatibility with the assignment of an Application Context Name identical to the one specified in RFC 1095.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is the list of choices that make ISO's management protocol usable on the Internet. It was rewritten in 1990 to point at the finished ISO standards and to drop material that had moved elsewhere.

sections.title: Why the ISO Management Standards Were Chosen
sections.content:
The memo is the output of the OSI Internet Management Working Group of the IETF, and as directed by the Internet Activities Board in RFC 1052 it addresses the need for a long-term network management system based on ISO CMIS/CMIP. Now that CMIS/CMIP had been voted an International Standard, it had become a stable basis for product development.

The profile specifies how to apply CMIP to the management of both IP-based and OSI-based Internet networks. Network management using ISO CMIP to manage IP-based networks is referred to as CMIP Over TCP/IP, or CMOT. Network management using ISO CMIP to manage OSI-based networks is referred to as CMIP. The memo specifies the protocol agreements necessary to implement CMIP and the accompanying ISO protocols over OSI, TCP and UDP transport protocols.

It must be read together with the documents defining the ISO standards an implementor needs: ASN.1, Association Control (ACSE), Remote Operations (ROSE), CMIS and CMIP with their addenda. The specification of a lightweight presentation layer protocol is required for use with the CMOT section of the profile. The SMI, MIB-I, MIB-II and OIM-MIB-II are used with the management system.

The choice of a set of protocol standards together with the further agreements needed to implement them is commonly called a profile. The selection policy is to use existing standards from the international standards community and the Internet community. Existing ISO standards and draft standards in the area of OSI network management form the basis of the profile, and other ISO application layer standards, ROSE and ACSE, support the ISO management protocol. To ensure interoperability, the memo makes certain choices and restrictions about the options and parameters the standards provide. The profile draws on the technical work of the OSI Network Management Forum and of the Network Management Special Interest Group of NIST, and wherever possible references or stays consistent with the agreements those groups reached.
sections.plainLanguage: ISO management was chosen because it had become a finished International Standard, which gives product builders something stable to work from. This document is the Internet's set of concrete choices on top of it.

sections.title: The Two Protocol Suites
sections.content:
The CMOT protocol suite is made of seven protocols: ISO ACSE, ISO DIS ROSE, ISO CMIP, the lightweight presentation protocol (LPP), UDP, TCP and IP. The CMIP protocol suite is made of six: ISO ACSE, ISO DIS ROSE, ISO CMIP, ISO Presentation, ISO Session and ISO Transport. The two figures in the RFC show how these stack up, with the management application processes at the top, then CMISE from ISO 9595 and 9596, then ACSE from ISO 8649 and 8650 alongside ROSE from ISO DIS 9072-1 and 9072-2. Below that the CMOT suite uses the Lightweight Presentation Protocol of RFC 1085 over TCP and UDP over IP, while the CMIP suite uses ISO Presentation, ISO Session and ISO Transport in turn.

A CMOT-conformant system must implement ACSE, ROSE, CMIP, LPP and IP, and must support the use of LPP over either UDP or TCP. It may support LPP over both on the same system. A CMIP-conformant system must implement ACSE, ROSE, CMIP, ISO Presentation, ISO Session and ISO Transport.
sections.plainLanguage: CMOT puts the ISO management protocol on top of a lightweight presentation protocol over TCP or UDP. CMIP leaves the ISO presentation, session and transport protocols in place. Both share ACSE, ROSE and CMIP.

sections.title: Association Types and Negotiation
sections.content:
CMISE requires four ACSE services: A-ASSOCIATE, A-RELEASE, A-ABORT and A-P-ABORT. The rest of the CMIP protocol uses the RO-INVOKE, RO-RESULT, RO-ERROR and RO-REJECT services of ROSE.

There are four types of association that may be negotiated between a managing and a managed system. In an Event association, the managed system may send M-EVENT-REPORTs and no other CMIP protocol data units are allowed. In an Event/Monitor association, as for Event, the managing system may also issue M-GET requests and receive M-GET responses. In a Monitor/Control association, the managing system may issue M-GET, M-SET, M-CREATE, M-DELETE and M-ACTION requests, and no event reporting is allowed. In a Full Mgr/Agent association all functions must be supported. A conformant system must support at least one of these types. A system may play both the managing and the managed role, but not on the same association.

The negotiation uses the A-ASSOCIATE and A-RELEASE services, and the Application Context Name determines the requestor's role in the association and the type of the association. Seven Application Context Names are registered for CMOT and CMIP: one for backwards compatible negotiation with RFC 1095 implementations, and six for the manager and agent forms of the four association types.

The negotiation rules are these. A managed system may only request an Event association, and must create an Event association if it has an event to report and no suitable association already exists. Managing systems may request any association type. An association is created by the requesting system issuing an A-ASSOCIATE request with the requestor's AE-TITLE and the desired application context, and the responding system returns either an A-ASSOCIATE response with the requestor's AE-TITLE and the application context it wishes to accept, or an A-ASSOCIATE response rejecting the association. Managed systems may negotiate downward, from Full to Monitor/Control, Event/Monitor or Event, by returning the new application context in the A-ASSOCIATE response, and from Event/Monitor to Event. When a managing system receives an application context in an A-ASSOCIATE response that differs from the one it sent, it may proceed with the new context or refuse it by issuing an A-RELEASE request.

A-RELEASE is used when the requestor does not agree with the new context. A-ABORT is used for invalid negotiation, and if it were used to terminate an association there would be the potential for loss of information such as pending events or confirmations. A-ABORT must nevertheless be used when a protocol violation occurs or where an association is not yet established.
sections.plainLanguage: When a manager and a managed system connect, they agree how much they will do over that connection: only send alerts, also allow reading values, also allow changing them, or everything. The agreement is carried in a name that both sides recognise.

sections.title: Agreements on CMIS and CMIP Services
sections.content:
The general agreements on users of CMIS are those in the OIW Stable Agreements, with additional agreements here. A system need only implement the services and service primitives required for the association types it supports. Current and Event times shall use 1 millisecond granularity. If the system generating the protocol data unit does not have the current time but does have the time since the last boot, GeneralizedTime can be used, with the time since last boot added to the base time 0001 Jan 1 00:00:00.00 using the Gregorian calendar algorithm, where all years have 365 days except those divisible by 4 and not by 400, which have 366. Using the year 1 as the base year prevents confusion with the current time. If no meaningful time is available, the year 0 shall be used in GeneralizedTime to indicate that fact.

The specific agreements on users of CMIS are those in the OIW Stable Agreements, with more here. Event time shall be mandatory for all events. Both the managed Object Class and managed Object Instance parameters must be present in the M-EVENT-REPORT Confirmed, M-GET, M-SET, M-ACTION, M-CREATE and M-DELETE service response and confirmation primitives.

The CMIS and CMIP implementers agreements in the OIW Stable Implementers Agreements, plus those mandated by the CMIP standard, are used for both CMOT and CMIP, with additional agreements: an implementation is required to support all filter items except subsetOf, supersetOf, nonNullSetIntersection and substrings; the managedObjectInstance field must be present in the ProcessingFailure Error protocol data unit; and the managedObjectClass field must be present in the NoSuchArgument Error protocol data unit.

The services required by CMIP are those in the OIW Stable Implementors Agreements, with more here. Application contexts shall be as defined in Section 4.1, and the values and defaults of parameters given to the presentation service are specified in RFC 1085 for CMOT and in the NIST Stable Implementers Agreements for CMIP. CMOT implementations shall be supported by the Lightweight Presentation Protocol, which may use either TCP or UDP; when UDP is used, an implementation need not accept LPP protocol data units whose length exceeds 484 octets. CMOT implementations will not require the session protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC also pins down small details that would otherwise differ between implementations: how times are written, which fields a reply must carry, and how long a message may be when it travels over UDP.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section of RFC 1189 says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The document defines protocol agreements and conformance requirements rather than behaviour, and it points to the ISO standards and the OIW Stable Agreements document for the rest.
sections.plainLanguage: This document has almost nothing to say about security. Its security section says only that security issues are not discussed here.
